title: Injecting clocks, randomness and services
summary: Turn hidden inputs into constructor dependencies, and write the fakes that tests use.

steps.title: An interface seam
body: For a class with several methods that need the time, pass a clock once, in the constructor:
class SystemClock : IClock { public DateTime UtcNow => DateTime.UtcNow; }
class FixedClock(DateTime at) : IClock { public DateTime UtcNow => at; }
Production wires `SystemClock`; tests use `FixedClock`. .NET 8+ ships the same idea as `TimeProvider`.

code: public DateTime UtcNow { get; private set; } = start;
public void Advance(TimeSpan by) => UtcNow += by;
steps.explain: A fake clock you can move forward lets one test check a month passing in microseconds.

steps.title: Kinds of test double
body: The object you hand in during a test is a **test double**. Names worth knowing:
- **Stub**: returns canned answers (`FixedClock`, a price lookup that always says 9.99).
- **Fake**: a working, simpler implementation (an in-memory repository instead of SQL).
- **Spy**: records how it was called so the test can check afterwards (a sender that stores messages).
- **Mock**: a spy with built-in expectations, usually from a library.

Prefer stubs and fakes for **inputs**, spies for **outputs** you must verify (an email was sent). Do not assert on every internal call: that couples tests to implementation and makes refactoring painful.

steps.prompt: A test checks that `Checkout` called `repository.GetById` exactly twice, then `cache.Set` once. What is the risk?
options: The test breaks when you refactor the internals, even if behaviour is still correct
Nothing, more assertions are always better

steps.title: Inject the randomness
prompt: `CouponService` hands out coupon codes using `new Random()`, so tests cannot predict them. Refactor:
- `interface IRandom { int Next(int max); }` (returns 0 to max-1)
- `string NewCode()` builds 4 characters, each `Alphabet[random.Next(Alphabet.Length)]`, with `const string Alphabet = "ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ23456789"`
The tests use their own `IRandom` that returns 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
template: Dojo.Eq("wraps at the end of the alphabet", "Z234", new CouponService(new DojoCounting(23)).NewCode());

steps.title: Fake the store, spy the mailer
prompt: `Signup` is given and already uses constructor injection. Write the two doubles the tests need:
- `class InMemoryUsers : IUserStore` (a fake): `Exists` and `Add` backed by a `HashSet<string>`
- `class SpyMailer : IMailer` (a spy): records every address passed to `Welcome` in `public List<string> Sent { get; } = new();`
starter: interface IUserStore { bool Exists(string email); void Add(string email); }
solution: interface IUserStore { bool Exists(string email); void Add(string email); }
template: var dojoSignup = new Signup(new InMemoryUsers(), dojoMail);
Dojo.Eq("welcome sent once per new user", new List<string> { "ada@x.io", "bob@x.io" }, dojoMail.Sent);
